walkthroughs.body_html: Classical theism, articulated by Augustine, Anselm and Aquinas, ascribes to God omnipotence, omniscience, omnibenevolence, eternity, immutability, simplicity and aseity. Aquinas argues these attributes follow from God's being subsistent existence itself (ipsum esse subsistens). Process theologians like Charles Hartshorne dissent, holding God to be in some respects mutable and affected by creation.

The Lateran Council (1215) defined that God created 'from nothing' both spiritual and corporeal creatures. This contrasts with Plato's Timaeus (where the Demiurge shapes pre-existing matter) and with pantheistic emanation. Genesis 1, the Wisdom literature, and 2 Maccabees 7:28 form the biblical basis. Augustine's Confessions XI explores creation 'with' time rather than 'in' time.

Providence is general (the ordering of nature) and special (the guidance of individuals). The problem of evil, sharpened by Epicurus and Hume, asks how an all-good and all-powerful God permits suffering. Augustine's free-will defence and Hick's Irenaean 'soul-making' theodicy give two main Christian replies; Plantinga's free-will defence develops the logical version.
